terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see the route, the moved position, the team lines and the radio log your functions read.

tasks.title: High and low on the route
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `grid_refs.py`, write a function called `height_range` that takes a list of heights and gives back two values, the lowest and then the highest, as a tuple. For tonight's route it gives back `(240, 760)`. Print what it gives back for `route_heights`.

Check calls `height_range` with heights of its own and looks at what it gives back: a tuple of two numbers, in that order.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on giving back two values.
Work out the lowest and the highest of the list.
Give back both in one `return`, the lowest first.
Print what it gives back and check the round brackets.
hints: A function gives back one value, but that value can be a tuple holding two.
Two values with a comma between them, after `return`, make a tuple. `min` and `max` give the two numbers.

tasks.title: Move a position
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a function called `moved` that takes a grid reference, a tuple of two numbers (how far east, then how far north), and how far to go east and north. It gives back the new grid reference as a new tuple. For the casualty at `(312, 845)`, 4 east and -2 north, it gives back `(316, 843)`. Print what it gives back for `casualty`, 4 and -2.

Check calls `moved` with grid references and distances of its own and looks at what it gives back: a tuple of two numbers.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on unpacking and on why a tuple cannot change.
Take the grid reference apart into two names.
Add each distance to its own number.
Give back a new tuple, east first.
hints: A tuple cannot be changed, so the new position is a new tuple made from the old one's numbers.
Two names on the left of `=` take a tuple of two values apart, one value each, in order. Then make the new tuple from the two sums.
The shape is `easting, northing = point` and then `return (easting + east, northing + north)`.

tasks.title: Send each team to its square
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a function called `team_lines` that takes a list of teams and a list of squares, the same length, and gives back a list of lines that pair them in order, the first team with the first square and so on. For tonight it gives back `['Team A to C4', 'Team B to D1', 'Team C to B5']`. Print each line it gives back for `teams` and `squares`.

Check calls `team_lines` with lists of its own, two empty ones too, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on `zip`.
Make an empty list for the lines.
Go through both lists together with `zip`, with one name for the team and one for the square.
Add a line on each round, and give back the list after the loop.
hints: One loop goes through both lists at once, a team and its square on each round. A loop inside a loop would pair every team with every square.
`zip` gives one tuple per position, and two names after `for` take each tuple apart.
The shape is `for team, square in zip(teams, squares):` with `lines.append(f"{team} to {square}")` inside, after `lines = []`.

tasks.title: When we last heard them
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, write a function called `last_heard` that takes a radio log, a list of `(time, call sign)` tuples in the order they came, and a call sign. It gives back the time of the last call from that call sign, or `None` when it never called. For tonight's log and `"Bravo two"` it gives back `21:40`. Print what it gives back for `radio_log` and `"Bravo two"`.

Check calls `last_heard` with logs and call signs of its own, one that never called, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on unpacking in a loop.
Start a name for the last time at `None`.
Go through the log, taking each call apart into a time and a call sign.
When the call sign matches, keep its time. Give back the last time after the loop.
hints: Keep the latest matching time in a name of its own, and give it back after the loop. A later match replaces an earlier one.
Two names after `for` take each call apart. Give them names that are not the same as the function's parameters, or the call sign you were given is lost.
The shape is `last = None`, then `for time, heard in log:` with `if heard == call_sign:` and `last = time` inside, and `return last` after the loop.
